title: Le Blanc: Vázquez is wrong; Durandus meant no grace through Christ at all
source_text: XIII. Sed legenti & expendenti Durandum patet Vasquem in eo falli, & mentem Durandi esse, hominem per naturae vires, & absque auxilio quocunque gratiae per Christum implere posse divina praecepta. Etenim sententiam suam probat hoc argumento. Illud quod homo naturaliter facit, sine gratia per seipsum facere potest: sed gentes quae legem non habent, naturaliter quae legis sunt faciunt, ut dicitur, Rom. 2. Ergo praecepta legis sine gratia impleri possunt. Unde patet Durando idem esse sine gratia facere, quod naturaliter & per seipsum facere. Qui autem aliquid facit mediante aliquo gratiae per Christum auxilio, illud dici non potest naturaliter & per seipsum facere, etiamsi alioqui gratia habituali & justificante careat. Adde quod Durandus ad eandem distinctionem scribens quaestione secunda, objicit sibi illa Christi verba, sine me nihil potestis facere. Ad quae respondet verba ista intelligenda esse de generali influentia Dei, qua rerum principia in esse conservat, sine qua nihil esset, aut fieret.
pass_a_gloss: XIII. But to one reading and weighing Durandus it is plain that Vasques is mistaken in this, and that the mind of Durandus is that man by the strength of nature, and without any help of grace through Christ whatever, can fulfil the divine precepts. For he proves his opinion by this argument. That which man does naturally, he can do without grace by himself: but the gentiles which have not the law, do naturally the things which are of the law, as is said, Rom. 2. Therefore the precepts of the law can be fulfilled without grace. Whence it is plain that for Durandus to do without grace is the same as to do naturally and by oneself. But he who does something by means of some help of grace through Christ, cannot be said to do it naturally and by himself, even if otherwise he lacks habitual and justifying grace. Add that Durandus writing on the same distinction, question two, objects to himself those words of Christ, without me ye can do nothing. To which he answers that those words are to be understood of the general influence of God, by which he preserves the principles of things in being, without which nothing would be, or be done.
pass_b_english: Anyone who reads Durandus carefully can see that Vázquez is wrong here. Durandus means that man, by the strength of nature and without any help of grace through Christ, can fulfil God's precepts. He proves his view with this argument: 'What man does naturally he can do of himself without grace. But the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things of the law, as Romans 2 says. So the precepts of the law can be fulfilled without grace.'

So for Durandus to act without grace is the same as to act naturally and of oneself. But a man who does something through some help of grace from Christ cannot be said to do it naturally and of himself, even if he lacks habitual and justifying grace.

Besides, in question 2 of the same distinction Durandus raises against himself Christ's words, 'Without me you can do nothing.' He replies that they must be understood of God's general influence, by which he keeps the principles of things in being, and without which nothing would exist or happen.
